title: Web Framework Landscape: Gin vs Echo vs Fiber vs Chi
summary: Go has no single blessed web framework because `net/http` is already good — so the ecosystem is a spectrum from thin routers to batteries-included frameworks. **Gin** and **Echo** are ergonomic, high-level frameworks with radix-tree routers and rich middleware. **Chi** is a thin, idiomatic router that stays 100% `net/http`-compatible. **Fiber** is the fastest option but is built on `fasthttp`, so it is NOT `net/http`-compatible — a tradeoff that costs you the entire standard middleware ecosystem. And since Go 1.22, the stdlib `ServeMux` supports method + wildcard patterns, so often the answer is no framework at all.
nestedConcepts: when the stdlib is enough (Go 1.22 mux)

subtopics.title: Chi: an idiomatic net/http router
subtopics.explanation: Chi is a lightweight router whose handlers are plain http.HandlerFunc and whose middleware is the standard func(http.Handler) http.Handler. It adds a fast trie router, route groups, and URL params via chi.URLParam, but never wraps or replaces the standard types. Because it is pure net/http, any stdlib-compatible middleware or handler drops straight in. Understanding Chi first anchors the whole framework landscape, because it is the baseline the others deviate from.

subtopics.title: Gin: ergonomic framework with a radix router
subtopics.explanation: Gin wraps every request in its own *gin.Context, which bundles the ResponseWriter, Request, params, binding helpers, and JSON rendering. Routing uses a fast radix (compressed prefix) tree, and middleware is gin.HandlerFunc — func(*gin.Context) — not the stdlib signature. This ergonomics-first design is why Gin has the biggest ecosystem, but it also shows the first real divergence from net/http that shapes the framework landscape.

subtopics.title: Echo: batteries-included, Gin-like
subtopics.explanation: Echo is philosophically close to Gin: its own echo.Context, a radix router, and a rich set of built-in middleware (CORS, JWT, rate limiting). Its distinctive touch is that handlers return an error (func(c echo.Context) error), centralizing error handling. Like Gin it uses net/http under the hood but exposes a non-stdlib handler signature, reinforcing the framework-vs-router axis of the landscape.

subtopics.title: Fiber: fastest, built on fasthttp
subtopics.explanation: Fiber offers an Express-like API and top raw throughput because it is built on valyala/fasthttp instead of net/http. fasthttp reuses request/response objects and buffers to avoid allocations, which is why it wins benchmarks. But its RequestCtx is a completely different type — there is no http.Request or http.ResponseWriter — so Fiber sits off to the side of the landscape, incompatible with the standard ecosystem.

subtopics.title: fasthttp is not net/http
subtopics.explanation: This is the single most important gotcha in the landscape. fasthttp reuses its RequestCtx and byte buffers across requests for speed, so its values are only valid during the handler and cannot be treated as http.Request/http.ResponseWriter. Consequently no standard middleware (func(http.Handler) http.Handler) works on Fiber, and any library expecting *http.Request (OpenTelemetry, gorilla, oauth2 handlers) must be re-implemented. You trade the entire net/http ecosystem for raw speed — that tradeoff defines Fiber's place in the landscape.

subtopics.title: When the stdlib is enough (Go 1.22 mux)
subtopics.explanation: Since Go 1.22 the standard http.ServeMux understands method and path-wildcard patterns like "GET /users/{id}", read via r.PathValue. Combined with the func(http.Handler) http.Handler middleware pattern, this covers routing, params, and 404/405 for the majority of services with zero dependencies. The stdlib mux is the low-dependency anchor of the landscape: reach for a framework only when its ergonomics or built-ins clearly earn their weight.

foundations.overview: Choosing a Go web framework is really about choosing where on a spectrum you want to sit. At one end is the standard library (net/http + Go 1.22 mux) and thin routers like Chi, which add convenience without ever leaving the http.Handler world. In the middle are Gin and Echo: full frameworks that trade the stdlib handler signature for ergonomic contexts, binding, and large middleware libraries. At the far end is Fiber, which abandons net/http entirely for fasthttp to win benchmarks. The decision hinges less on raw speed and more on net/http compatibility, ecosystem reuse, and long-term maintainability.
foundations.formalDefinition: A Go HTTP router maps (method, path pattern) pairs to request handlers and dispatches incoming requests to the matching one. A router/framework is 'net/http-compatible' if its handlers and middleware operate on http.ResponseWriter and *http.Request (or types that embed them), so it interoperates with the standard func(http.Handler) http.Handler ecosystem. Chi and the stdlib mux are net/http-compatible; Gin and Echo are net/http-based but expose their own Context handler signature; Fiber is fasthttp-based and thus net/http-incompatible.
foundations.whyItMatters: The framework decision is one of the earliest and stickiest in a Go project — it dictates how every handler is written, which middleware you can reuse, and how easily you can adopt libraries like OpenTelemetry or oauth2. Picking Fiber for a benchmark number can quietly cost you months when you later need standard middleware that simply does not exist for fasthttp.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture a dial from 'pure stdlib' to 'own universe'. Stdlib mux and Chi are near zero: everything speaks http.Handler, so the whole ecosystem plugs in. Gin and Echo turn the dial partway: their own Context is more ergonomic but their middleware is bespoke, so you live inside their ecosystem. Fiber turns the dial to the far end: maximum speed, but it is a separate universe (fasthttp) where net/http libraries do not exist.
foundations.runtimePerspective: Gin, Echo, and Chi all run on the standard http.Server: one goroutine per connection/stream, r.Context() cancelled on disconnect/timeout. Their routers differ (radix tree for Gin/Echo, trie for Chi, the stdlib's own pattern matcher for ServeMux) but routing is O(path length) in all cases and rarely the bottleneck. Fiber runs on fasthttp's server, which pools RequestCtx and buffers across requests to cut allocations — that pooling is exactly why its objects must not escape the handler.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Gin powers many popular open-source APIs and internal services thanks to its ecosystem; Echo appears in service templates that want built-in middleware; Chi is favored by teams that want idiomatic net/http with light routing (used by projects that value stdlib compatibility); Fiber shows up in latency-sensitive edge services; and an increasing number of Go 1.22+ services use the stdlib mux with a small middleware helper and no framework at all.
foundations.businessImpact: The right choice keeps engineers productive and dependencies auditable; the wrong one (typically over-optimizing for benchmark throughput) can lock a team out of standard security, tracing, and auth libraries, raising the cost and risk of every future integration and slowing delivery.
foundations.engineeringImpact: net/http-compatible choices (stdlib, Chi) maximize reuse and testability (httptest works directly) and keep handlers portable. Framework-specific choices (Gin, Echo) concentrate ergonomics but couple your code to that framework's Context and middleware. Fiber's incompatibility means you must reimplement or find fasthttp-specific versions of everything the stdlib ecosystem provides.
foundations.performanceImpact: In realistic services the framework is almost never the bottleneck — the database, downstream calls, and serialization dominate. Fiber's fasthttp edge (fewer allocations, object reuse) is measurable in synthetic 'hello world' benchmarks but usually vanishes under real I/O. Gin, Echo, Chi, and the stdlib mux are all fast enough that maintainability, not routing speed, should drive the decision.
commonUseCases: JSON REST APIs where a radix router + binding (Gin/Echo) speeds up development
Idiomatic services that want light routing but full net/http compatibility (Chi)
Latency-critical edge/proxy services willing to give up net/http (Fiber)
Small or dependency-averse services using the Go 1.22 stdlib mux directly

commonMisconceptions.myth: Fiber is 'just a faster Gin' so it is a safe default.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Fiber is built on fasthttp, not net/http. Its *fiber.Ctx is not http.Request/http.ResponseWriter, so standard func(http.Handler) http.Handler middleware and net/http libraries (OpenTelemetry, oauth2, gorilla) do not work with it.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You must pick a framework to get decent routing in Go.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Since Go 1.22 the standard ServeMux supports method + wildcard patterns ("GET /users/{id}", r.PathValue) and returns 404/405 automatically, covering most routing needs with zero dependencies.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Framework routing speed is what determines a service's throughput.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Routing is O(path length) and negligible next to DB/network/serialization. Real throughput is dominated by I/O, so maintainability and ecosystem should drive the choice, not micro-benchmarks.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Chi is a heavy framework like Gin or Echo.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Chi is a thin router: its handlers are plain http.HandlerFunc and its middleware is the standard func(http.Handler) http.Handler, so it composes with the entire net/http ecosystem.

interactiveExamples.title: The same route in four stacks, side by side
interactiveExamples.explanation: Comparing the identical GET /users/{id} route across the stdlib mux, Chi, Gin, and Fiber makes the divergence concrete: the stdlib and Chi use http.ResponseWriter/*http.Request, Gin uses *gin.Context, and Fiber uses *fiber.Ctx (fasthttp). Only the first two are net/http-compatible.

code.caption: One route, four handler signatures. Only the stdlib and Chi variants speak net/http.
code.expectedOutput:
// GET /users/42 -> body "user 42" in every case
// but only stdlib & Chi handlers are func(w, r) and reusable across the net/http ecosystem

interactiveExamples.title: Reusing one stdlib middleware — and where it stops
interactiveExamples.explanation: A single func(http.Handler) http.Handler logging middleware drops straight onto the stdlib mux and Chi (r.Use), works on Gin only via gin.WrapH adapters, and cannot be used on Fiber at all because there is no *http.Request to pass.

code.caption: One middleware, four fates — a direct consequence of net/http compatibility.
code.expectedOutput:
// stdlib & Chi: Logging runs, prints "GET /users/42 128µs"
// Gin: needs an adapter; Fiber: cannot use it at all

interactiveExamples.title: The fasthttp reuse trap: don't let *fiber.Ctx escape
interactiveExamples.explanation: Because fasthttp pools RequestCtx and buffers, storing c or the []byte from c.Body()/c.Params() beyond the handler reads memory that has been reused by a later request. This is the class of bug that never happens with net/http, whose *http.Request is per-request.

code.caption: fasthttp's speed comes from reuse; that reuse is the footgun net/http never has.
code.expectedOutput:
// Buggy version: process() may see a DIFFERENT request's body under load
// Fixed version: process() always sees the correct copied bytes

checkpoints.prompt: Which Go web stack is NOT compatible with the standard func(http.Handler) http.Handler middleware ecosystem?
checkpoints.explanation: Fiber is built on fasthttp, whose *fiber.Ctx is not http.Request/http.ResponseWriter, so standard func(http.Handler) http.Handler middleware cannot be applied. The stdlib mux and Chi both use net/http types directly, so they are fully compatible.

checkpoints.prompt: Using the Go 1.22 stdlib mux, what does the client receive for GET /users/42?
options: 404 not found (mux needs a third-party router for params)
checkpoints.explanation: Since Go 1.22 the standard ServeMux supports method + path-wildcard patterns. "GET /users/{id}" matches GET /users/42 and r.PathValue("id") returns "42", so the body is "user 42" with a 200 — no third-party router required.

checkpoints.prompt: This Fiber handler stores the request body for later async processing. Under load, process() sometimes sees the wrong bytes. Why?
options: c.Body() returns a fasthttp buffer that is reused by later requests; you must copy it
checkpoints.explanation: fasthttp pools and reuses its RequestCtx and byte buffers across requests for speed. c.Body() points into that pooled buffer, so once the handler returns the bytes may be overwritten by the next request. You must copy them (append([]byte(nil), c.Body()...)) before letting them escape the handler.

checkpoints.prompt: Register a standard net/http logging middleware on a Chi router (Chi middleware IS func(http.Handler) http.Handler).
checkpoints.explanation: Chi's Use registers middleware, and Chi middleware has the exact standard signature func(http.Handler) http.Handler, so a plain net/http middleware like Logging is passed directly: r.Use(Logging). No adapter is needed, unlike Gin or Fiber.

codeLab.title: Write one net/http handler, mount it on stdlib mux and Chi
codeLab.instructions: Because Chi and the stdlib mux both use net/http types, a single func(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request) handler works on both unchanged. Implement `GetUser` so that GET /users/{id} responds with body `user <id>`. It must read the path value in a way that works when mounted on EITHER router. Hint: the stdlib mux exposes r.PathValue; Chi (v5) is configured in the harness to also populate r.PathValue, so use r.PathValue("id").
hints: Both the Go 1.22 ServeMux and Chi v5 populate r.PathValue("id"), so you never need a router-specific accessor.
The handler signature is func(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request) — the same portable shape Chi and the stdlib both accept.
Write the body with fmt.Fprintf(w, "user %s", id); no WriteHeader needed since 200 is the default.

codeLab.title: Build a router-agnostic middleware and prove it works on stdlib and Chi
codeLab.instructions: Implement `WithHeader(key, value string) func(http.Handler) http.Handler` — a standard net/http middleware that sets a response header, then calls the next handler. Because it uses the standard signature, the SAME middleware must work when applied to a stdlib mux handler and when registered via Chi's r.Use. Return a middleware whose returned handler sets w.Header().Set(key, value) before delegating to next.
hints: The outer function returns func(next http.Handler) http.Handler; the inner returns an http.HandlerFunc.
Set the header with w.Header().Set(key, value) BEFORE calling next.ServeHTTP, since headers must precede the body.
Chi's r.Use accepts exactly this func(http.Handler) http.Handler shape, which is why the same middleware works on both routers.

debuggingLab.title: A net/http middleware won't compile on Fiber
debuggingLab.symptom: You copied a standard logging/auth middleware (func(http.Handler) http.Handler) from a Gin/Chi project into a Fiber app and app.Use(Logging) fails to compile — the types don't match and there is no *http.Request to hand it.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Fiber is built on fasthttp, not net/http. app.Use expects a fiber.Handler = func(*fiber.Ctx) error, whereas Logging is func(http.Handler) http.Handler operating on http.ResponseWriter/*http.Request. Those types are fundamentally different — fasthttp has no http.Request — so the standard middleware cannot be adapted without reimplementation. This is the concrete cost of Fiber's net/http incompatibility: the entire func(http.Handler) http.Handler ecosystem is unavailable.
commonMistakes: Assuming Fiber is a drop-in faster Gin and shares net/http middleware.
Trying to pass http.ResponseWriter/*http.Request that fasthttp does not have.
Reaching for an 'adaptor' expecting perfect fidelity — fiber/adaptor exists but wraps at a boundary and can copy/allocate, negating the fasthttp speed advantage.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Rewrite the logging as a native Fiber middleware (func(*fiber.Ctx) error that calls c.Next()), or use Fiber's built-in logger — and recognize that any net/http-only library must be reimplemented for fasthttp.

solution.expectedOutput:
// compiles; log line: GET /users/42 96µs
// note: this middleware is Fiber-only and cannot be reused on net/http routers

theory.question: What does it mean that Fiber is built on fasthttp and not net/http, and why does it matter?
theory.directAnswer: Fiber uses valyala/fasthttp as its HTTP engine instead of the standard net/http. fasthttp gains speed by pooling and reusing its RequestCtx and byte buffers across requests, so its handler receives a *fiber.Ctx that is NOT an http.Request/http.ResponseWriter. This matters because the entire Go middleware and library ecosystem is built around func(http.Handler) http.Handler and *http.Request — none of it works with Fiber without reimplementation. It also introduces a footgun: values from c.Body()/c.Params() must be copied before they escape the handler, because the buffer is reused by the next request.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A framework whose transport layer is fasthttp, a net/http-incompatible, allocation-minimizing HTTP implementation.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To win throughput benchmarks by reusing request/response objects and avoiding per-request allocations.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: fasthttp hands the handler a pooled RequestCtx; Fiber wraps it as *fiber.Ctx. After the handler returns, the ctx and its buffers are reset and reused for a future request.

theory.whyImportant: It is the single most consequential compatibility fact in the Go web landscape and a favorite interview probe to see if a candidate understands ecosystem tradeoffs, not just benchmark numbers.
theory.realWorldExample: A team picks Fiber for speed, then can't add OpenTelemetry HTTP instrumentation (net/http-based) or reuse their existing auth middleware, and must rewrite everything against fasthttp.

followUps.question: Can you use net/http middleware with Fiber at all?
followUps.answer: Only via fiber/adaptor, which bridges at a boundary and can add copying/allocation, partly negating the fasthttp performance advantage.

followUps.question: Why must you copy c.Body()?
followUps.answer: It points into a pooled fasthttp buffer that is reused by the next request; copy with append([]byte(nil), c.Body()...) before letting it escape the handler.

theory.question: How do Gin, Echo, Chi, and the stdlib mux differ in their middleware models and net/http compatibility?
theory.directAnswer: The stdlib mux and Chi use the standard model: handlers are func(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request) and middleware is func(http.Handler) http.Handler, so both are fully net/http-compatible and reuse the whole ecosystem. Gin and Echo are net/http-based servers but expose their own context: Gin handlers/middleware are func(*gin.Context) (call c.Next() to continue), and Echo handlers are func(echo.Context) error with its own middleware type — so their middleware is framework-specific, not the stdlib signature. Fiber is off the net/http axis entirely (fasthttp). In short: stdlib and Chi = standard signature and reusable; Gin/Echo = bespoke context, own middleware; Fiber = different universe.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The differing handler/middleware signatures and their relationship to net/http.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Gin/Echo trade the stdlib signature for ergonomic contexts (binding, rendering, built-in middleware); Chi and the stdlib prioritize compatibility.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Gin/Echo wrap each request in their Context and run their own middleware chain; Chi and the stdlib call http.Handler.ServeHTTP directly through func(http.Handler) http.Handler layers.

theory.whyImportant: Knowing which stacks preserve net/http compatibility tells you which middleware and libraries you can reuse — a core maintainability concern.
theory.realWorldExample: Moving a service from Gin to Chi lets the team drop Gin-specific middleware and reuse standard net/http middleware and httptest-based tests unchanged.

followUps.question: Why do Gin and Echo use their own Context?
followUps.answer: To bundle params, binding, validation, and response helpers ergonomically and to allow c.Next()-style flow control in middleware.

followUps.question: Is Chi middleware really identical to stdlib middleware?
followUps.answer: Yes — Chi middleware is func(http.Handler) http.Handler, so any standard middleware works via r.Use with no adapter.

theory.question: With Go 1.22's enhanced ServeMux, when is a framework unnecessary and when is one still worth it?
theory.directAnswer: Since Go 1.22 the stdlib ServeMux supports method + wildcard patterns ("GET /users/{id}", read via r.PathValue) and returns 404/405 automatically, so for services that mainly need routing, path params, and a small middleware stack, no framework is needed — you get zero dependencies and full net/http compatibility. A framework still earns its place when you want built-in ergonomics and features the stdlib lacks: request binding/validation, rendering helpers, route groups with per-group middleware, a large curated middleware library (CORS, JWT, rate limiting), or a specific performance profile (Fiber). The decision is: start with the stdlib (or Chi for grouping/light routing) and adopt Gin/Echo only when their built-ins clearly save meaningful work.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The tradeoff between the dependency-free stdlib mux and full frameworks after Go 1.22.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go 1.22 closed the biggest historical gap (method + wildcard routing) that pushed people to frameworks.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: ServeMux now matches patterns like 'POST /items/{id}/tags/{tag}' and exposes segments via r.PathValue; middleware remains the standard wrapping pattern.

theory.whyImportant: It demonstrates judgment: choosing the lowest-dependency option that meets requirements, rather than reaching for a framework reflexively.
theory.realWorldExample: A new microservice ships on the stdlib mux with a 40-line middleware helper, avoiding a framework dependency and keeping httptest-based tests trivial.

followUps.question: What does the stdlib mux still NOT give you?
followUps.answer: Built-in request binding/validation, response rendering helpers, route-group middleware sugar, and a curated middleware library — you assemble those yourself or via small packages.

followUps.question: Where does Chi fit relative to the stdlib mux?
followUps.answer: Chi adds nested route groups, per-group middleware, and richer routing while staying net/http-compatible — a natural step up before a full framework.

scenario.question: A team benchmarked frameworks and wants to adopt Fiber for a public REST API because it topped a 'hello world' throughput test. What advice do you give?
scenario.directAnswer: Push back on optimizing for a synthetic benchmark. In a real REST API, throughput is dominated by the database, downstream calls, and JSON serialization — not the router — so Fiber's fasthttp edge usually disappears under real I/O. Meanwhile Fiber's net/http incompatibility is a lasting cost: you lose the standard func(http.Handler) http.Handler middleware ecosystem and net/http libraries (OpenTelemetry HTTP instrumentation, oauth2 handlers, gorilla helpers, httptest-based tests), and you inherit the fasthttp buffer-reuse footgun (must copy c.Body()). I'd recommend the stdlib mux (Go 1.22) or Chi for full compatibility and maintainability, or Gin/Echo if the team wants built-in ergonomics — and only choose Fiber if profiling proves the HTTP layer is a real bottleneck AND the team is prepared to live in the fasthttp ecosystem.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A choice between benchmark-driven speed (Fiber) and ecosystem compatibility/maintainability (stdlib/Chi/Gin/Echo).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Micro-benchmarks tempt teams to optimize the layer that is rarely the bottleneck.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Real services spend most time in I/O and serialization; the router is O(path length) and negligible.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows engineering judgment: weighing long-term maintainability and ecosystem reuse against a headline number.
scenario.realWorldExample: A public API on Fiber later needs distributed tracing and standard auth middleware, forcing a costly migration back to a net/http stack.

followUps.question: How would you prove the router isn't the bottleneck?
followUps.answer: Profile the real service with pprof and load tests; you'll typically see time dominated by DB/RPC and JSON encoding, with routing a rounding error.

followUps.question: When WOULD Fiber be justified?
followUps.answer: A latency-critical, minimal-logic edge/proxy service where per-request allocations matter, the ecosystem needs are small, and the team accepts fasthttp's constraints.

scenario.question: You're inheriting a Gin service and need to add OpenTelemetry tracing, per-route rate limiting, and reuse an existing standard net/http auth middleware. How do you approach middleware compatibility?
scenario.directAnswer: Gin is net/http-based but uses its own gin.HandlerFunc = func(*gin.Context), so standard middleware isn't a drop-in. Use the official otelgin middleware for tracing (Gin-native), Gin's or a library's rate-limit middleware (keyed by API key/IP, returning 429), and for the existing net/http auth middleware, adapt it at the boundary using gin.WrapH/gin.WrapF or by invoking the standard middleware's ServeHTTP with c.Writer and c.Request inside a small gin.HandlerFunc, then calling c.Next(). Prefer Gin-native equivalents where they exist to avoid awkward context bridging; only adapt when the net/http middleware is bespoke and worth reusing. Longer term, if broad net/http reuse is a recurring need, consider Chi or the stdlib mux where these middlewares work unchanged.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Bridging standard net/http middleware into Gin's context-based chain.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Gin's ergonomic *gin.Context signature diverges from func(http.Handler) http.Handler.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: gin.WrapH/WrapF adapt http.Handler/HandlerFunc into Gin handlers; you can also call next.ServeHTTP(c.Writer, c.Request) then c.Next().

scenario.whyImportant: It tests practical knowledge of framework-specific vs standard middleware and how to interoperate without a rewrite.
scenario.realWorldExample: Adding otelgin for tracing while wrapping a legacy net/http auth middleware via gin.WrapH so the team avoids reimplementing auth.

followUps.question: What's the risk of adapting net/http middleware into Gin?
followUps.answer: The adapter may not integrate with Gin's context flow (c.Next, c.Abort) cleanly, so short-circuiting and per-context values can behave unexpectedly; test carefully.

followUps.question: How do you rate-limit per route in Gin?
followUps.answer: Register a limiter middleware on a route group (r.Group) so only those routes carry it, keyed by client identity, returning 429 with Retry-After.

systemDesign.question: You must standardize the HTTP stack for a new set of Go microservices. Design a decision guide for choosing among stdlib mux, Chi, Gin/Echo, and Fiber, and justify a default.
systemDesign.directAnswer: Frame it as a decision tree driven by compatibility and needs, not raw speed. (1) Default to the Go 1.22 stdlib ServeMux + a small shared middleware package for services that need routing, path params, and standard cross-cutting concerns — zero dependencies, full net/http compatibility, trivial httptest testing. (2) Step up to Chi when you need nested route groups, per-group middleware, and richer routing while keeping net/http compatibility. (3) Choose Gin or Echo when teams want built-in ergonomics — request binding/validation, rendering helpers, and a large curated middleware library — and are fine coupling handlers to a framework context. (4) Choose Fiber only for latency-critical, low-logic edge services where per-request allocation matters AND you accept losing the net/http ecosystem and the fasthttp buffer-reuse rules. Standardize a shared middleware module, structured logging, tracing (OpenTelemetry), health/readiness endpoints, server timeouts, and graceful shutdown across all of them. Recommended org default: stdlib mux or Chi, because compatibility and maintainability compound across many services more than a routing micro-benchmark ever will.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An organization-level policy for selecting a Go HTTP stack per service type.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Consistency lowers cognitive load and enables shared middleware, tooling, and on-call runbooks across services.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A decision tree keyed on net/http compatibility, needed ergonomics/features, and proven performance requirements, with a compatible default.

systemDesign.whyImportant: The stack choice is sticky and multiplied across many services; a compatibility-first default protects future integrations (tracing, auth, security) and reduces migration risk.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: An org standardizes on Chi + a shared middleware module; every service reuses the same logging/auth/tracing and identical httptest patterns, and no service is locked out of net/http libraries.

followUps.question: How do you enforce consistency across teams?
followUps.answer: Ship a shared bootstrap/middleware module (logging, tracing, recovery, timeouts, health endpoints) and a service template, so the stack choice and cross-cutting concerns are standardized by default.

followUps.question: What triggers revisiting the default for a given service?
followUps.answer: Profiling that proves the HTTP layer is a genuine bottleneck, or a feature need (heavy binding/validation) that a framework clearly serves better than the stdlib.

coding.question: Implement a Chain helper for standard net/http middleware so `Chain(A, B, C)(h)` equals `A(B(C(h)))` (first argument is outermost). Signature: `func Chain(mws ...Middleware) Middleware` where `type Middleware func(http.Handler) http.Handler`. This is exactly the model Chi and the stdlib share.
coding.thoughtProcess: A Middleware is func(http.Handler) http.Handler. To make the first argument the outermost wrapper, apply the slice in reverse: wrap the final handler with the last middleware first, then work outward, so the first middleware ends up on the outside and runs first on the way in. Return a closure that performs this wrapping for any handler h.
coding.lineByLine: Middleware is the standard func(http.Handler) http.Handler shared by Chi and net/http. Chain returns a Middleware (a closure over the mws slice). Inside, we start from the passed-in handler h and iterate the slice from the last index down to zero; each step wraps the current h with mws[i]. Because the last middleware is applied first, the first middleware is applied last and therefore sits outermost, so it runs first on the way in — matching A(B(C(h))).
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) to build the chain for n middleware; O(1) per-request overhead per layer.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n) handler wrappers for n middleware.

followUps.question: Why iterate in reverse instead of forward?
followUps.answer: Forward wrapping would make the last argument outermost. Reverse wrapping puts the first argument on the outside, which is the conventional 'first = runs first' ordering.

followUps.question: Does this work with Chi?
followUps.answer: Yes — Chi middleware is the same func(http.Handler) http.Handler type, so Chain composes Chi middleware identically and the result can be passed to r.Use or used to wrap a mux.

coding.question: Write a router-agnostic net/http handler `Health` for GET /healthz that returns 200 and body `ok`, plus a test using httptest that drives it through a Go 1.22 ServeMux. Demonstrate that pure net/http handlers are trivially testable without a running server.
coding.thoughtProcess: Keep the handler as a plain func(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request) so it works on any net/http-compatible router. Register it on a stdlib mux with the method+path pattern, then use httptest.NewRequest and httptest.NewRecorder to invoke ServeHTTP and assert status and body — no network needed, which is a key advantage of net/http-compatible stacks.
coding.lineByLine: Health is a standard handler: it sets 200 with WriteHeader then writes the body 'ok'. In the test, we build a Go 1.22 mux and register Health under 'GET /healthz'. httptest.NewRecorder gives an in-memory ResponseWriter and httptest.NewRequest builds a request without a socket. Calling mux.ServeHTTP routes the request to Health and captures the result in rr, which we assert on. Because everything is net/http, this test needs no listening server — the same test would fail to be this simple against Fiber's fasthttp types.

followUps.question: Why does httptest work here but not directly on Fiber?
followUps.answer: httptest produces http.ResponseWriter/*http.Request; Fiber handlers take *fiber.Ctx (fasthttp), so you'd need fasthttp's test utilities instead of the standard httptest package.

followUps.question: How would you add a readiness endpoint?
followUps.answer: Register 'GET /readyz' with a handler that checks dependencies (DB ping) and returns 503 when not ready, flipping to 200 once healthy.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Treat the router choice as an interface boundary: keep business logic in handlers that depend only on standard types where possible, so the router is swappable. Prefer net/http-compatible stacks (stdlib mux, Chi) so a shared middleware module (logging, recovery, request ID, tracing, timeouts) is reused across services. If a framework (Gin/Echo) is used, isolate framework-specific code (context accessors, binding) in a thin layer so core logic stays portable. Expose /healthz, /readyz, and /metrics regardless of stack.
productionDeepDive.performance: The router is rarely the bottleneck: routing is O(path length) and dwarfed by DB/RPC and JSON work. Gin/Echo (radix), Chi (trie), and the stdlib mux are all fast enough for typical services. Fiber/fasthttp wins synthetic 'hello world' throughput via object/buffer reuse, but the advantage usually shrinks under real I/O. Optimize serialization, connection pooling (reuse a tuned http.Client Transport for outbound), and avoid per-request allocations in hot middleware before considering a fasthttp move; profile with pprof to confirm where time actually goes.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: On net/http-based stacks (stdlib, Chi, Gin, Echo) each request runs in its own goroutine with a per-request *http.Request, so handler state is naturally isolated and shared state must be guarded. Always pass r.Context() downstream for cancellation. On Fiber/fasthttp, the RequestCtx and its buffers are POOLED and reused across requests, so you must never let c, c.Body(), or c.Params() escape the handler goroutine without copying — a concurrency hazard that does not exist with net/http.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Set explicit server timeouts (ReadHeaderTimeout/ReadTimeout/WriteTimeout/IdleTimeout) regardless of framework, since none add safe defaults for you (Fiber exposes its own timeout config on fasthttp). Add recovery middleware (Gin/Echo include one; on stdlib/Chi add your own) so a panic becomes a clean 500. Implement graceful shutdown: net/http stacks use srv.Shutdown(ctx); Fiber uses app.Shutdown(). Wrap downstream calls with timeouts, bounded retries, and circuit breakers.
productionDeepDive.observability: Prefer stacks where standard instrumentation drops in: OpenTelemetry's net/http instrumentation and RED metrics middleware work directly on stdlib/Chi and via otelgin/otelecho for Gin/Echo. Fiber needs fasthttp-specific instrumentation (fiber/otelfiber, built-in logger), so tracing/metrics integrations are a distinct effort. Propagate a request ID via context, emit structured logs, and record per-route latency histograms.
productionDeepDive.security: Set ReadHeaderTimeout to defend against slow-loris on any stack. Size-limit bodies (http.MaxBytesReader on net/http; fasthttp has its own limits). Prefer stacks where audited net/http security middleware (secure headers, CSRF, auth, oauth2 handlers) is reusable — a compatibility win for stdlib/Chi and, via adapters, Gin/Echo. On Fiber, security middleware must be fasthttp-native, so validate that equivalents exist and are maintained. Terminate TLS at the server or a proxy; never log full tokens.

caseStudies.company: Fintech API team standardizing on Chi
caseStudies.problem: Multiple services each picked a different framework, blocking reuse of a shared auth/tracing middleware and forcing per-service integration work.
caseStudies.solution: Standardized on Chi (net/http-compatible) with a shared middleware module and service template; existing standard net/http middleware and httptest suites worked unchanged.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Gave up some batteries-included ergonomics (binding helpers) that Gin/Echo provide, adding a little boilerplate per handler.
caseStudies.lessons: For a fleet of services, net/http compatibility compounds: one middleware module and one testing style beat a per-framework routing micro-optimization.

caseStudies.problem: A CPU-bound, low-logic request-forwarding service needed maximum throughput and minimal per-request allocation.
caseStudies.solution: Adopted Fiber/fasthttp for the hot path, accepting the loss of net/http libraries and enforcing strict copy-before-escape rules for c.Body()/c.Params().
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Could not reuse the org's net/http tracing/auth middleware and had to add fasthttp-specific instrumentation and careful buffer handling.
caseStudies.lessons: Fiber pays off only when the HTTP layer is truly the bottleneck and ecosystem needs are minimal; the buffer-reuse model demands disciplined coding to avoid subtle data bugs.

keyTakeaways: Go's web landscape is a spectrum: stdlib mux and Chi stay pure net/http; Gin and Echo are net/http-based frameworks with their own Context; Fiber is off the axis on fasthttp.

Fiber is fast because fasthttp pools and reuses RequestCtx/buffers, but it is NOT net/http-compatible: standard func(http.Handler) http.Handler middleware and net/http libraries do not work, and you must copy c.Body() before it escapes the handler.

Chi's handlers and middleware are the exact standard types (http.HandlerFunc and func(http.Handler) http.Handler), so it composes with the entire net/http ecosystem; the stdlib mux (Go 1.22) adds method + wildcard routing with zero dependencies.
Routing is almost never the bottleneck — I/O and serialization dominate — so choose primarily on net/http compatibility, ecosystem reuse, and maintainability, not synthetic benchmark throughput.
Gin and Echo trade the stdlib signature for ergonomics (binding, rendering, curated middleware); reuse standard middleware in them only via adapters like gin.WrapH.

Decision guide: default to the stdlib mux or Chi for compatibility; pick Gin/Echo when built-in ergonomics clearly pay off; pick Fiber only for latency-critical, low-logic services where you accept leaving the net/http ecosystem.
